title: BEFORE YOU HIT SHARE: What If the Lie You’re Spreading Is Helping the Politician You Love—but Wounding the Christ You Claim to Follow?
paragraphs: BEFORE YOU HIT SHARE: What If the Lie You’re Spreading Is Helping the Politician You Love—but Wounding the Christ You Claim to Follow?
When Christians become so loyal to a political side that they stop asking whether something is true, deception has already won something far more valuable than an argument.
Your thumb is hovering over the “Share” button.
The headline makes your blood boil.
It confirms what you already suspected.

It makes the politician you distrust look terrible. It makes the politician or movement you favor look vindicated. Thousands of people have already reacted. Friends are sharing it. Someone wrote, “WAKE UP!” Another said, “The media will never tell you this!”
And something inside you whispers:
So you do.
Maybe you never opened the article.
Maybe you watched only fifteen seconds of a two-minute video.
Maybe the photograph came from another event.
Maybe the quotation was clipped before the speaker finished the sentence.
Maybe the accusation came from an anonymous page citing another anonymous page citing someone who provided no evidence at all.
Maybe it is true.
Maybe it is partly true.
Maybe it is completely false.
But there is a question Christians desperately need to recover before another political post leaves our hands:
Do I actually know?
Because the moment truth becomes less important to us than whether a story hurts “their side” or helps “our side,” we are no longer merely discussing politics.
We are dealing with discipleship.
And Scripture is frighteningly clear about this.
Exodus 23:1 says:
לֹא תִשָּׂא שֵׁמַע שָׁוְא
Lo tissa shema shav.
The Hebrew carries the prohibition against taking up, bearing, or spreading a false report.
“Do not spread false reports.”
Notice how painfully contemporary that sounds.
God gave that command thousands of years before Facebook.
Before algorithms.
Before edited reels.
Before anonymous political pages.
Before fabricated screenshots.
Before artificial intelligence could generate convincing images, voices, and videos.
But God already understood the human heart.
A false report does not need technology to become dangerous.
It only needs someone willing to carry it.
And sometimes...
that carrier is a Christian.
That should disturb us.
Not because Christians are forbidden from participating in politics. Scripture does not command believers to become intellectually passive, socially indifferent, or silent about injustice.
Christians may investigate wrongdoing.
Christians may expose corruption when evidence establishes it.
Christians may criticize leaders.
Christians may disagree passionately about policies.
Christians may call evil what God calls evil.
John the Baptist confronted Herod.
The prophets confronted kings.
Nathan stood before David and said, “You are the man.”
Biblical faithfulness has never required cowardice before political power.
But there is an enormous difference between speaking truth to power and spreading something merely because we hope it is true about someone we oppose.
Truth does not become holy because it attacks your enemy.
And a lie does not become righteous because it benefits your cause.
Read that again.
A lie does not become righteous because it benefits your cause.
Imagine standing before Jesus with every post you have ever shared displayed before you.
Not only the pornography you refused to watch.
Not only the profanity you refused to speak.
Not only the sins Christians usually talk about.
The posts.
The screenshots.
The accusations.
The edited clips.
The rumors.
The “breaking news” you never verified.
The story that made you angry enough to stop checking whether it was accurate.
Would you be comfortable saying:
“Lord, I did not know whether it was true...
but it helped my side.”
That sentence should terrify every disciple of Jesus.
Because our Lord did not describe Himself as merely someone who likes truth.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” — John 14:6
Truth is not an optional accessory to Christianity.
Truth is inseparable from the character of the Christ we worship.
This is why Paul writes in Ephesians 4:25:
ἀποθέμενοι τὸ ψεῦδος
apothemenoi to pseudos
“Having put away falsehood...”
and then:
λαλεῖτε ἀλήθειαν
laleite alētheian
“Speak truth.”
Paul’s command is not:
Speak truth unless an election is approaching.
Speak truth unless the other candidate is dangerous.
Speak truth unless your favorite politician needs defending.
Speak truth unless your political tribe is losing.
Speak truth unless the lie exposes somebody you believe deserves to be exposed.
No.
Put away falsehood.
Speak truth.
Why?
Because Christianity does not give us permission to borrow the weapons of darkness in order to defend what we believe is light.
And this is where deception becomes incredibly subtle.
You may genuinely believe you are defending your country.
You may genuinely believe a political leader is corrupt.
You may genuinely believe another leader has been falsely accused.
You may genuinely believe an election, policy, scandal, investigation, or controversy has enormous moral consequences.
Any of those conclusions might be right.
Or wrong.
The Christian obligation remains the same:
Do not bear false witness.
Your certainty about somebody’s character does not automatically authenticate every accusation made against them.
A politician may actually be dishonest while a particular story about that politician is still false.
A politician may actually have done something wrong while a viral photograph supposedly proving it is miscaptioned.
A political movement may have serious problems while a quotation attributed to one of its leaders is fabricated.
That distinction matters.
Because Christians are not permitted to manufacture evidence for conclusions they already believe.
Proverbs 18:13 warns:
“To answer before listening—that is folly and shame.”
And only a few verses later comes another devastating reminder:
“The first to state his case seems right until another comes and cross-examines him.” — Proverbs 18:17
That sounds almost like Scripture was preparing believers for social media.
You see the first post.
It seems convincing.
Then the fuller video appears.
Then the original document appears.
Then the quotation is traced to its source.
Then the photograph turns out to be several years old.
Then the supposedly shocking statistic turns out to mean something completely different in context.
Then someone quietly deletes the original post.
But the lie has already traveled.
And perhaps your name helped carry it.
James tells us the tongue can set an enormous forest on fire.
Today the “tongue” can have a touchscreen.
One click.
One repost.
One screenshot.
One accusation.
And thousands of people can receive something you never bothered to establish as true.
This is why discernment cannot mean:
“I agree with it.”
Discernment means being willing to discover that something you wanted to believe is false.
That hurts.
Because political deception frequently feeds on something deeper than ignorance.
It feeds on identity.
We begin thinking:
These are my people.
That is my candidate.
This is my movement.
Those people are destroying everything.
Then something dangerous happens.
We stop evaluating information according to truth and start evaluating truth according to tribe.
If it damages them, we believe it immediately.
If it damages us, we demand impossible levels of proof.
If our opponent commits wrongdoing, it proves everything we believed.
If our preferred leader commits wrongdoing, suddenly everybody mentioning it must be part of a conspiracy.
That is not discernment.
That is partiality wearing religious clothing.
And Christians should be especially difficult to manipulate precisely because our ultimate identity does not belong to a political party.
Paul wrote:
ἡμῶν γὰρ τὸ πολίτευμα ἐν οὐρανοῖς ὑπάρχει
Hēmōn gar to politeuma en ouranois hyparchei.
“Our citizenship is in heaven.” — Philippians 3:20
That does not mean earthly citizenship is meaningless.
It means earthly politics must never become ultimate.
Jesus is not running for office.
Jesus does not need propaganda.
Jesus does not need fabricated statistics.
Jesus does not need manipulated photographs.
Jesus does not need us to lie for Him.
And no politician deserves what belongs to Christ alone.
No candidate died for your sins.
No political party rose from the grave.
No administration purchased you with blood.
No president, prime minister, senator, governor, mayor, activist, influencer, or political movement will sit upon the throne described in Revelation.
Jesus will.
So when loyalty to a politician makes a Christian comfortable with dishonesty, something has moved into a place in the heart where it does not belong.
And perhaps this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because it is easy to condemn fake news when other people spread it.
It is harder when the false story says exactly what we desperately want to hear.
Before sharing something political, ask yourself:
Have I read beyond the headline?
Have I found the original source?
Is the quotation complete?
Is the photograph actually from the event being discussed?
Does the article provide evidence?
Have reputable independent sources confirmed the central claim?
Am I sharing verified information—or merely somebody’s interpretation of it?
And perhaps most importantly:
If this exact story attacked the politician I support, would I demand more evidence before believing it?
That question can expose the heart.
But what happens if you discover that you already shared something false?
This is where the Gospel enters.
Not humiliation.
Not pretending.
Not deleting the post quietly and hoping nobody noticed.
Repentance.
If we have misled people, knowingly or carelessly, the Christian response is not to protect our image.
It is to love truth more than our reputation.
Delete or correct the false information.
Acknowledge the mistake.
Where appropriate, tell the people you misled that the information was inaccurate.
And do not say:
“Well, the politician is probably corrupt anyway.”
That is not repentance.
Repentance says:
“I shared something I could not substantiate. It was wrong. I am correcting it.”
Do you realize how powerful that could be?
Imagine Christians becoming known online not as the easiest demographic to outrage...
but the hardest people to deceive.
Imagine believers checking sources before sharing accusations.
Imagine Christians refusing to circulate manipulated media even when it destroys someone they politically oppose.
Imagine a believer publicly saying:
“I was wrong. I shared misinformation. Please disregard my previous post.”
The world might laugh.
But heaven does not despise humility.
We follow a Savior who said:
“You will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” — John 8:32
And perhaps some of us need freedom today.
Freedom from political obsession.
Freedom from outrage addiction.
Freedom from the need to always prove the other side evil.
Freedom from defending people who have slowly become idols.
Freedom from believing everything that confirms our fears.
Freedom from being manipulated by people who discovered that anger keeps us clicking.
And freedom from the pride that prevents us from saying:
I was deceived.
There is grace for that confession.
Peter was deceived by his own confidence.
Thomas struggled to believe.
Paul persecuted the Church while convinced he was serving God.
Human beings can be profoundly sincere and profoundly mistaken.
But Jesus rewrites stories.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Peter denied Jesus beside a fire and later proclaimed Him before crowds.
Paul went from persecuting Christians to preaching the Christ he once opposed.
The Gospel does not merely forgive sinners.
It transforms them.
And that means Jesus can transform how we behave online too.
Maybe you shared things you should not have shared.
Maybe anger became your addiction.
Maybe politics has consumed your conversations more than Jesus.
Maybe you have defended a politician more passionately than you have defended the truth.
Maybe you discovered that some of the information you trusted was false.
Come back.
Not to another political tribe.
Come back to Christ.
Repentance is not political defeat.
Repentance is spiritual freedom.
Jesus is not asking you to become politically ignorant.
He is calling you to become faithful.
Investigate.
Test.
Listen.
Read.
Verify.
Correct yourself when necessary.
Refuse slander.
Refuse manufactured outrage.
Refuse falsehood even when falsehood would help your preferred candidate.
And when wrongdoing is genuinely established, speak truthfully, courageously, fairly, and without becoming what you claim to oppose.
Because the question is bigger than:
Who wins the argument?
The deeper question is:
When people encounter what you share, can they still trust the name of Christ attached to your profile?
Someone reading this right now remembers a post.
Maybe even several.
Do not run from the conviction.
Take it to Jesus.
You can simply write “Jesus, lead me in truth.”
If you once shared misinformation and God has convicted you to become more careful, your testimony might help another believer admit the same thing.
And if you know someone whose political loyalty is slowly swallowing their Christian witness, do not use this article as a weapon against them.
Save this too.
The next outrageous headline will come.
The next scandal will come.
The next viral accusation will come.
And before your thumb touches “Share,” come back and remember:
Truth does not need your impatience.
And invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite Christians who have grown lukewarm.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
It does not make you more Christian.
It does not prove that you love Jesus.
Christ alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.

But if this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life and you prayerfully want to help us reach more people with Scripture-centered content, your voluntary support can become an act of generosity and stewardship offered for God’s glory.
Choose truth.
Share truth.
Repent when you spread falsehood.
Love people enough to verify accusations before destroying reputations.
Love your enemies enough not to lie about them.
Love your neighbors enough not to deceive them.
And love Jesus enough that no politician ever becomes too important for you to admit the truth.
Because one day every campaign will end.
Every administration will end.
Every political dynasty will end.
Every trending hashtag will disappear.
Every viral post will become yesterday’s noise.
But Christ will still be King.
So before you share the next political scandal, remember the line that may save your Christian witness:
Never let your loyalty to a politician make you betray the Truth who died for you.
